subject: Anatomy
summary: The spinal cord is a vital part of the central nervous system, extending from the brainstem down the vertebral column. It transmits sensory and motor information between the brain and the body, and mediates reflexes. Damage can lead to significant neurological deficits.

sections.p: The spinal cord is a long, cylindrical bundle of nervous tissue that serves as the main communication pathway between the brain and the rest of the body. It is protected by the vertebral column, meninges, and cerebrospinal fluid. Understanding its anatomy is crucial for diagnosing and managing neurological conditions.
b: It is part of the central nervous system (CNS).
Extends from the foramen magnum to the L1/L2 vertebral level in adults.
Mediates reflex actions independently of the brain.

sections.p: The spinal cord is housed within the vertebral canal. It tapers inferiorly into the conus medullaris, from which the filum terminale extends. It has cervical and lumbar enlargements to accommodate the increased nerve supply to the limbs.
b: Composed of gray matter (H-shaped core) and white matter (surrounding tracts).
Gray matter contains neuronal cell bodies, dendrites, and unmyelinated axons.
White matter consists of myelinated axons organized into ascending (sensory) and descending (motor) tracts.
Sensory neurons whose axons form the dorsal roots are bipolar.
Meninges (dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater) surround and protect the spinal cord.

sections.p: The spinal cord is intimately related to the vertebral column, spinal nerves, and surrounding structures. Its position within the vertebral canal means that vertebral injuries or diseases can directly impact spinal cord function.
b: Anteriorly: Vertebral bodies and intervertebral discs.
Posteriorly: Laminae and spinous processes of vertebrae.
Laterally: Pedicles and intervertebral foramina, through which spinal nerves exit.
Spinal nerves emerge segmentally, forming 31 pairs (8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal).

sections.p: The spinal cord receives its blood supply from longitudinal arteries and segmental arteries. Disruption of this supply can lead to ischemia and neurological deficits, highlighting the importance of collateral circulation.
b: Anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord.
Two posterior spinal arteries supply the posterior one-third.
Segmental medullary arteries (radicular arteries) reinforce the longitudinal arteries, especially the great anterior medullary artery (artery of Adamkiewicz).

sections.p: The spinal cord itself is the origin and termination point for numerous nerve pathways. It processes sensory input and generates motor output, with specific regions dedicated to different functions.
b: Dorsal roots carry sensory (afferent) information to the spinal cord.
Ventral roots carry motor (efferent) information away from the spinal cord.
Preganglionic parasympathetic neurons originate from the sacral spinal cord (S2-S4).
Preganglionic sympathetic neurons originate from the thoracic and lumbar spinal cord (T1-L2).

sections.p: The spinal cord has two primary functions: transmitting nerve impulses and mediating reflexes. Its white matter tracts carry information to and from the brain, while its gray matter integrates information for reflexes.
b: Conduit for sensory information (e.g., touch, pain, temperature, proprioception) to the brain.
Conduit for motor commands from the brain to muscles and glands.
Mediates reflex arcs, which are neural pathways controlling reflexes that synapse in the spinal cord.
The spinal cord dorsal columns of the white matter do NOT carry pain, temperature, or crude touch.

sections.p: Spinal cord injuries are devastating, often leading to permanent neurological deficits. Understanding the level and type of injury is critical for prognosis and management. Conditions like meningocele also highlight developmental defects.
b: Spinal cord compression is a medical emergency requiring urgent diagnosis and intervention.
Traumatic injuries (e.g., fractures, dislocations) are common causes of spinal cord damage.
Non-traumatic causes include tumors (often found in the spinal cord in adults), infections, and vascular events.
Meningocele involves herniation of meninges through a vertebral defect, with the spinal cord remaining in its normal position, so neurological deficit is uncommon.
Symptoms of injury vary by level: cervical injuries affect all four limbs, thoracic injuries affect the trunk and lower limbs.

t.b: What is the level and completeness of the injury? Assesses motor strength, sensation, and reflexes to localize the lesion.

What is the cause of compression or injury? Identifies fractures, disc herniations, tumors, or inflammation affecting the spinal cord. If unavailable, plain X-rays can show bony abnormalities, but CT is better for bone detail.

sections.p: When considering spinal cord anatomy and pathology, always think about the functional implications of a lesion at a specific level. Differentiate between upper and lower motor neuron signs, and understand the distinct pathways for different sensory modalities.
b: Remember the difference in spinal cord termination in children (L3) versus adults (L1/L2).
Differentiate between complete and incomplete spinal cord injuries based on sacral sparing.
Understand the clinical presentation of anterior spinal artery syndrome versus posterior cord syndrome.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden weakness or numbness in limbs
Loss of bladder or bowel control
Severe back pain radiating to the legs

faq.q: What is the difference between the spinal cord and the vertebral column?
faq.a: The vertebral column is the bony structure (backbone) that protects the spinal cord, which is the nervous tissue inside it.

faq.q: Can the spinal cord heal after injury?
faq.a: The spinal cord has limited capacity for regeneration, and severe injuries often result in permanent neurological deficits, though research into repair is ongoing.

A reflex arc is a neural pathway that controls a reflex, involving a sensory neuron, an interneuron (often), and a motor neuron, with a synapse in the spinal cord, allowing for rapid, involuntary responses.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic neurological exam allow rapid localisation of spinal cord injury and identification of red‑flags that demand urgent intervention.
b: Onset: sudden (trauma, vascular) vs. progressive (tumour, infection).
Mechanism: flexion‑distraction, penetrating, fall; note level of impact.
Pain: radicular, midline, mechanical, night‑time worsening.
Motor: weakness pattern, gait changes, sphincter control.
Sensory: level of numbness, type (pain‑temp vs. proprioception).
Autonomic: hypotension, bradycardia, temperature dysregulation, bowel/bladder dysfunction.
Past medical: HIV, TB, diabetes, previous spine surgery, anticoagulants.

t.b: Determines strength in each myotome; a score <3 indicates functional weakness; helps map lesion level.
Assesses pain‑temperature (spinothalamic) and dorsal column function; a sensory level indicates lesion segment.
Tests dorsal column integrity; preserved vibration with loss of pain suggests posterior cord syndrome.
Hyperreflexia and Babinski sign indicate upper motor neuron lesion; absent reflexes suggest lower motor neuron involvement.
Evaluates sacral S2‑S4 integrity; present reflex suggests intact sacral pathways.

t.a: Rectal tone and voluntary anal contraction
t.b: Assesses conus medullaris or cauda equina involvement; loss indicates severe cauda syndrome.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Imaging and electrophysiology confirm the level, extent and aetiology of spinal cord pathology; laboratory tests identify systemic contributors.
b: MRI spine (T1, T2, STIR) – gold standard for cord contusion, haemorrhage, compression; hyperintense T2 signal >3 vertebral levels predicts poorer outcome.
CT spine – rapid assessment of bony fracture, disc fragment, foreign body; useful when MRI unavailable.
CT myelogram – delineates canal compromise when MRI contraindicated; contrast outlines subarachnoid space.
X‑ray (AP, lateral, flexion‑extension) – screens for instability; >3 mm translation suggests surgical fixation.
Somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEP) – assess functional integrity of dorsal columns; absent response indicates severe injury.
Motor evoked potentials (MEP) – evaluate corticospinal tract; reduced amplitude predicts motor deficit.

t.b: If >3 vertebral segments, higher risk of permanent deficit; guides prognosis and rehab planning.

t.a: CT evidence of burst fracture with canal compromise >50%
t.b: Indicates need for urgent decompression and stabilization.
Suggests dorsal column dysfunction; may influence surgical timing.
Correlates with motor weakness; helps monitor intra‑operative neuroprotection.
Elevated inflammatory markers raise suspicion for infection (TB, epidural abscess); treat accordingly.
Hyperglycaemia worsens secondary injury; optimise glucose control.

sections.p: Spinal cord injury is classified by neurological level, completeness and functional impact using internationally accepted scales.
b: ASIA Impairment Scale (AIS): A (complete), B (sensory incomplete), C (motor incomplete, <50% key muscles grade ≥3), D (motor incomplete, ≥50% key muscles grade ≥3), E (normal).
Neurological level – most caudal segment with normal sensory and motor function on both sides; defines motor/sensory zones of partial preservation (ZPP).
Frankel grade – older system correlating with AIS (A‑E).
Spinal Cord Injury–Related Pain (SCIP) classification – nociceptive vs. neuropathic, guides analgesic strategy.
American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) motor score – sum of 10 key muscles bilaterally (0‑100).
Spinal shock phase – flaccid paralysis, areflexia; resolves within days‑weeks, transition to spasticity indicates injury chronicity.

sections.p: Several pathologies mimic acute spinal cord injury; careful history, exam and targeted imaging separate them.
b: Spinal epidural abscess – fever, back pain, progressive neuro deficit; MRI with contrast shows rim‑enhancing collection.
Transverse myelitis – post‑infectious, often bilateral sensory loss; MRI shows longitudinally extensive T2 hyperintensity without compression.
Cauda equina syndrome – radicular pain, saddle anaesthesia, early bladder dysfunction; MRI shows nerve root compression below L2.
Brown‑Séquard syndrome – hemisection from penetrating trauma; ipsilateral motor loss, contralateral pain‑temp loss; MRI confirms unilateral cord damage.

t.b: Distinguishes compressive lesions (abscess, tumour) from intrinsic cord pathology (myelitis).

t.a: CSF analysis (cell count, protein, culture, PCR)
t.b: Elevated white cells, low glucose suggest infection; oligoclonal bands point to inflammatory demyelination.
Positive results support epidural abscess or tuberculous arachnoiditis; initiate antimicrobial therapy.
Detects metastatic disease causing vertebral collapse; guides oncologic management.

sections.p: Acute spinal cord injury requires rapid stabilization, prevention of secondary damage, and early definitive care while continuously monitoring neurologic status.
b: 1. Cervical immobilization with rigid collar and log‑roll transfer to avoid further cord movement.
2. Airway, breathing, circulation: ensure adequate oxygenation (SpO2 ≥ 94 %) and maintain MAP 85‑90 mmHg with fluids or vasopressors.
3. High‑dose methylprednisolone is no longer routine; give only if protocol exists and within 8 h, otherwise avoid due to infection risk.
4. Obtain emergent MRI (if available) to define level, compression, hemorrhage; if MRI unavailable, CT myelogram.
5. Surgical decompression and stabilization within 24 h for compressive lesions; choose posterior, anterior or combined approach based on level and pathology.
6. Continuous neurologic checks (ASIA motor and sensory scores) every 4 h for the first 24 h, then every 8 h.
7. Escalate to neurosurgery/trauma team if worsening deficit, hemodynamic instability, or respiratory compromise.
8. Initiate early rehabilitation and bladder/bowel management once medically stable.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Pharmacologic agents used in acute spinal cord injury have specific adverse profiles that must be anticipated and managed.
b: Vasopressors (norepinephrine, phenylephrine): may cause peripheral ischemia; monitor limb perfusion and titrate to MAP target.
High‑dose steroids (if given): increase risk of hyperglycemia, GI bleeding, and infection; give proton‑pump inhibitor and strict glucose control.
Anticoagulation for DVT prophylaxis (low‑molecular‑weight heparin): watch for bleeding at surgical sites; check platelet count and anti‑Xa if renal failure.
Opioids for pain: cause respiratory depression and constipation; use multimodal analgesia and bowel regimen.
Muscle relaxants (baclofen) for spasticity: may cause hypotonia and sedation; start low and monitor blood pressure.

sections.p: Early recognition of secondary complications guides timely escalation to intensive care or specialist input.
b: Neurogenic shock: hypotension with bradycardia and warm extremities; treat with fluids and norepinephrine, call senior intensivist.
Respiratory failure from high cervical injury: monitor tidal volumes, consider early intubation and ventilatory support.
Autonomic dysreflexia (injury ≥ T6): sudden hypertension, pounding headache; sit patient upright, remove stimulus, give nifedipine if severe.
Deep vein thrombosis: swelling, pain, Homan’s sign; if duplex unavailable, start therapeutic anticoagulation if no bleeding risk.
Pressure ulcers: stage I‑IV skin breakdown; involve wound‑care team when ulcer > stage II or infection suspected.

sections.p: Co‑morbid conditions alter presentation, investigations, and therapeutic choices in spinal cord injury.
b: HIV: increased infection risk; use prophylactic antibiotics peri‑operatively and monitor CD4 count.
TB meningitis or Pott’s disease: may mimic cord compression; obtain CSF analysis and chest X‑ray; treat TB before elective surgery.
Malnutrition: poor wound healing; give high‑protein enteral nutrition early.
Pregnancy: avoid supine hypotension; position left lateral tilt; use MRI without gadolinium; fetal monitoring during surgery.
Diabetes: hyperglycemia worsens neurologic outcome; maintain glucose 140‑180 mg/dL.
Renal failure: adjust LMWH dose, avoid nephrotoxic contrast; use non‑contrast CT if MRI contraindicated.
Alcohol withdrawal: risk of seizures; give benzodiazepines and monitor vitals.
Herbal remedies (e.g., St. John’s wort): may induce CYP enzymes, reducing steroid levels; ask patient to stop before admission.

sections.p: Management must be adapted for children, pregnant women, the elderly, people living with HIV, and settings with limited resources.
b: Children: use age‑appropriate immobilization devices; consider growth‑plate sparing surgical techniques; fluid resuscitation based on weight.
Pregnancy: prioritize maternal hemodynamics, fetal monitoring, and avoid teratogenic drugs; plan delivery after neurologic stabilization.
Elderly: higher risk of osteoporosis‑related fractures; use gentle traction and consider minimally invasive fixation.
People with HIV: screen for opportunistic infections, start antiretroviral therapy after acute phase, avoid drug interactions with protease inhibitors.
Low‑resource settings: if MRI unavailable, rely on CT and clinical exam; use plain radiographs for fracture classification; prioritize early transfer to higher‑level centre.

t.b: Ask mechanism of injury, time since onset, bladder/bowel function, prior neurologic disease, medication, substance use, and pregnancy status.
Inspect for deformity, palpate spinous processes, test motor (key muscles C5‑T1, L2‑S1), sensory (pinprick, light touch, vibration), reflexes (deep tendon, plantar), and assess sacral sparing.
MRI spine (compressive lesion, hemorrhage); CT if MRI not available; X‑ray for fracture classification; CBC, electrolytes, glucose, coagulation; urine output for neurogenic bladder.
Use clinical level (sensory dermatome) to guide surgical planning; obtain CT myelogram if MRI impossible.
Presence of voluntary anal contraction or sacral sensation (ASIA grade C/D) predicts better functional recovery.

facts: Spinal cord ends at L1–L2 vertebral level (conus medullaris) in adults.
Anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two‑thirds of the cord; posterior spinal arteries supply the posterior one‑third.
The great radicular artery (artery of Adamkiewicz) most commonly arises from T9–L2 and supplies the lower thoracic and lumbar cord.
ASIA Impairment Scale grades A (complete) to E (normal); motor score is 0–100, sensory score 0–224.
Brown‑Séquard syndrome: ipsilateral motor loss and proprioception, contralateral loss of pain and temperature below lesion.
Central cord syndrome: greater motor loss in upper limbs than lower limbs, often with sacral sparing.
Anterior cord syndrome: loss of motor, pain and temperature; vibration and proprioception preserved.
Cervical spinal cord injury can cause neurogenic shock: hypotension, bradycardia, warm extremities due to loss of sympathetic tone.

mnemonics.t: Spinal cord termination at L1–L2 (S), Anterior spinal artery supplies two‑thirds (A), Dermatomes: umbilicus = T10 (D).

vivas.q: Define Brown‑Séquard syndrome and describe the expected neurological findings below the lesion.
vivas.a: Hemisection of the cord; ipsilateral loss of motor function and proprioception, contralateral loss of pain and temperature.

vivas.q: At which vertebral level does the adult spinal cord terminate?
Explain the physiological basis of neurogenic shock in high cervical spinal cord injury.
vivas.a: Loss of sympathetic outflow leads to unopposed parasympathetic tone, causing hypotension, bradycardia, and warm, flushed skin.

vivas.q: Identify the incomplete syndrome that spares proprioception and vibration but loses motor and pain/temperature.
What clinical sign indicates an incomplete spinal cord injury and predicts a better prognosis?
vivas.a: Presence of sacral sparing (preserved voluntary anal contraction or sensation).

vivas.q: Name the artery that supplies the anterior two‑thirds of the spinal cord.
What is the immediate management priority in the first few hours after a traumatic spinal cord injury?
vivas.a: Immobilisation of the spine, maintenance of mean arterial pressure 85–90 mmHg, and prevention of secondary injury.

vivas.q: List the main incomplete spinal cord syndromes and a key clinical feature of each.
vivas.a: Brown‑Séquard (ipsi motor/proprioception, contra pain), Anterior cord (motor + pain loss, vibration spared), Central cord (greater upper‑limb weakness), Posterior cord (loss of vibration/proprioception).

vivas.q: Describe how to assess the sensory level in a patient with suspected spinal cord injury.
vivas.a: Test light touch and pinprick from distal to proximal on each side; the highest normal dermatome defines the sensory level.

vivas.q: Why is a high‑dose steroids regimen no longer recommended for acute spinal cord injury?
vivas.a: Evidence shows no functional benefit and increased risk of infection, GI bleeding, and hyperglycaemia.

vivas.q: How can you differentiate central cord syndrome from cervical spondylotic myelopathy on exam?
vivas.a: Central cord shows disproportionate upper‑limb weakness with relative lower‑limb preservation; spondylotic myelopathy often has progressive gait disturbance and bilateral signs.

vivas.q: What are the components of the ASIA motor score?
vivas.a: Ten key muscles (five upper, five lower) graded 0–5 on each side; total possible 100 points.

vivas.q: When is MRI indicated in acute spinal cord injury?
vivas.a: To assess cord compression, hemorrhage, disc herniation, and ligamentous injury when CT is inconclusive or surgery is planned.

vivas.q: Explain why sacral sparing is a good prognostic sign.
vivas.a: It indicates that some descending pathways are intact, correlating with higher likelihood of functional recovery.

vivas.q: What bedside test can assess dorsal column function?
vivas.a: Vibration with a 128‑Hz tuning fork and proprioception by moving a finger; loss suggests posterior column involvement.

vivas.q: In a patient with suspected spinal shock, what finding distinguishes it from neurogenic shock?
vivas.a: Spinal shock presents with flaccid paralysis and areflexia initially, whereas neurogenic shock shows hypotension and bradycardia without loss of reflexes.

mcqs.q: A 22‑year‑old male suffers a stab wound to the right thoracic spine. Which finding is expected ipsilaterally below the lesion?
o: Loss of pain and temperature sensation
mcqs.e: Ipsilateral corticospinal tract is damaged, causing motor loss on the same side.

mcqs.q: Which spinal segment supplies the dermatome at the level of the umbilicus?
A patient with a cervical cord injury develops hypotension, bradycardia, and warm extremities. The primary cause is:
mcqs.e: Loss of sympathetic tone leads to neurogenic shock.

mcqs.q: Which incomplete syndrome is characterised by loss of motor, pain and temperature, but preserved vibration?
mcqs.e: Anterior cord syndrome spares dorsal columns (vibration/proprioception).

mcqs.q: The artery of Adamkiewicz most commonly arises from which level?
mcqs.e: It usually originates between T9 and L2, supplying the lower thoracic/lumbar cord.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is the first step in the acute management of a suspected spinal cord injury?
In the ASIA exam, a motor score of 0‑5 is assigned to each muscle. How many key muscles are tested?
mcqs.e: Ten key muscles (five upper, five lower) are graded.

mcqs.q: Which clinical sign indicates an incomplete spinal cord injury with a better prognosis?
mcqs.e: Sacral sparing shows preserved descending pathways.

cases.v: A 30‑year‑old male is brought after a fall from a tree. He is alert, neck immobilised, and has flaccid paralysis of both legs, loss of pain and temperature below T6, but vibration sense is intact. Blood pressure 85/55 mmHg, heart rate 48/min.

qs.q: What is the most likely spinal cord syndrome?
What is the immediate management priority?
qs.a: Maintain MAP 85–90 mmHg, treat neurogenic shock with fluids and vasopressors, and keep spinal immobilisation.

qs.q: Which artery injury most likely explains this presentation?
qs.a: Compromise of the anterior spinal artery or its feeder (e.g., artery of Adamkiewicz).

cases.v: A 45‑year‑old woman presents after a motor‑vehicle collision. She has right‑sided weakness (3/5) in the arm and leg, loss of vibration on the right, and loss of pain and temperature on the left below C5. Reflexes are brisk on the right side.

qs.q: Which tracts are responsible for the contralateral loss of pain and temperature?
qs.a: Spinothalamic tract, which crosses within one or two segments.
CT scan of the cervical spine to assess bony injury, followed by MRI if cord compression is suspected.

mistakes: Confusing the level of spinal cord termination (L1–L2) with the lowest vertebral level of the lumbar spinal cord segments (L5).
Assuming loss of all sensation in Brown‑Séquard; pain and temperature loss is contralateral.
Prescribing high‑dose steroids routinely for acute cord injury despite current guidelines.
Neglecting to maintain MAP 85–90 mmHg in the first 24 h, leading to secondary ischemic injury.
Failing to document sacral sparing, which is a key prognostic indicator.
Using MRI as the first imaging in unstable trauma patients without prior cervical spine protection.
Mistaking spinal shock (reflex loss) for neurogenic shock (hemodynamic instability).
Overlooking the artery of Adamkiewicz as a source of ischemia in lower thoracic injuries.
